title: The equation that's key to finding alien life: 'We can't be alone'
excerpt: Sixty-five years on, Frank Drake’s seven-variable equation remains a vital roadmap for alien-hunting scientists, having inspired humanity’s first radio message to the stars
content:
It was humanity’s first dedicated message to the stars - a cosmic hello in the hope of contacting aliens. Now, 65 years after the Drake equation - a maths equation that led to that historic transmission was developed - the formula is still being used by scientists to tackle the biggest question of all… are we alone?

The Arecibo Message - a further attempt to communicate with aliens - was transmitted into space by radio telescope in Puerto Rico in November 1974. But the origin of the groundbreaking dispatch began in 1961, when visionary astrophysicist Frank Drake developed a formula for estimating the potential number of intelligent civilisations living among the stars.

The Drake equation plotted for the first time the different factors to be considered when looking for intelligent life. It also shaped the transmission’s coding and targeting. Frank’s daughter, Nadia Drake, explains: “The thing is, no one had thought to organise the question like that before, largely because thinking about finding aliens was mostly considered to be science fiction.

‌

“Dad didn't just stare skyward and wonder whether life-bearing worlds populate our cosmic horizons. He actually did the work to tackle that question scientifically. It initially seems quite complicated, but the maths is simple, and so is the logic - to calculate the number of detectable civilisations, you need to pin a value on seven variables.”

In science, a variable is, basically, anything that can change or be measured. Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Inside Science, Nadia adds: “Sixty five years later, the equation still has no answer, but it has become a roadmap. Pretty much every space mission or Earth-based experiment is designed to pin a value on at least one of the seven variables.”

Sophie Allan is the Head of Teaching and Learning at the National Space Centre in Leicester. She says Frank’s work came at a time when there was a huge uptick in interest in extraterrestrial life. She explains: “Radio telescopes were getting bigger and more sensitive. Astronomers started to realise they might be getting powerful enough to pick up radio signals from other human-like civilisations.

‌

“So if there were others in our galaxy, they reasoned we might be able to hear them. This was when there was a real flurry of interest in SETI - the search for extraterrestrial intelligence.”

Frank Drake was a US scientist, fascinated by the potential of galactic communications with other life forms. He realised that by breaking the cosmos down into bite-sized variables, it might be possible to calculate the number of detectable civilisations living among the stars.

Explains 43-year-old Sophie: “He understood we had to think about the factors that might influence whether intelligent life emerges. So - we need to know how many stars there are in a galaxy and the rate of star formation. He said we then need to know how many of those stars are going to have planets around them, because you can't have a civilisation without a planet.

‌

“But not all of those planets are going to be suitable for habitable life, so we need to think about what the number of planets within a solar system might be which could sustain life as we know it. Then - what fraction of them do we actually get life appearing on and, of that fraction, how many of those life generating planets are going to lead to intelligent life?

"After all, if we're ever going to be able to contact them they've got to get intelligent enough to build the technology and to be able to send radio signals out. And then, how long will those civilisations last? Are they going to stick around long enough to develop interstellar communication?”

Sophie, who has a degree in astrophysics, says Drake’s work became “the second most famous equation in science after E=mc2,” but was never intended to produce a concrete answer. She adds: “It was designed to be used as a conversation tool, to get people thinking - and it did. And still does.”

‌

Less than a decade later, it also formed the basis of an interstellar radio signal and the first attempt at humanity communicating with aliens. Known as the Arecibo message, it was beamed into space from the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico, towards the star cluster Messier 13 - about 25,000 light years away.

M13 was chosen, as it contains around 300,000 stars, meaning there were a huge number of potential targets. Scientists hoped any message might also be intercepted on its travels. Sophie explains: “The message was the next logical step in the SETI field and designed as both a demonstration and celebration of what humans could achieve.”

Frank Drake was a central figure in the design of the communication, which was broadcast not in words but images contained in a binary code represented by a series of zeros and ones.

‌

Experts reasoned that if it was intercepted and decoded, key information about Earth would emerge, including a representation of our solar system and elements on the periodic table, as well as details about our DNA and even a crude image of a human being. To date, no reply has been received, although scientists continually scan the cosmos listening for contact.

As well as keeping scientists occupied, the equation and the message has been referenced down the decades in a host of films and television programmes, including The X Files, Star Trek: Voyager, The Big Bang Theory and the Jodie Foster movie, Contact.

Sophie says: “I’m a space nerd. Intuitively, it feels like we can't be alone - there are so many planets and moons that could potentially develop life. But, while my heart says there must be something out there, at the moment we don’t have the scientific data. And if we are the only intelligent life that has ever emerged, we've got a lot of responsibility not to mess that up.

‌

"That said, you only have to step outside to get a glimpse of what there is beyond this little protective envelope - that’s why people remain fascinated by space. As a species, we seek connection, we seek stories and there would be no bigger story than being able to share your own with another civilisation.

"I think that’s the reason sci-fi has never gone away as a genre. And when the world feels [unstable] as it does at the moment, it's always good to remember that, actually, humans working together to solve problems can achieve incredible things - like Frank Drake.”

The scientist, who had an asteroid named after him, died in California in 2022, aged 92. Nadia Drake, herself now a science journalist based in the US, says the more her father learned about the potential for life on other worlds to exist, the more hopeful he got.

Herself a director of the SETI Institute in California, she adds: “He was an astute observer of the world around him. He noticed the little details, like blossoms emerging on the plum tree in our backyard. And while he would always say that we don't know the answer to the Drake equation until we know the answer, I think toward the end of his life, he let some hope creep in . . . . for the other worlds in our galaxy. Hope that, maybe, they could be as lucky and as beautiful as the planet that he loved most.”

‌

Space in 2026

We see space as a static place but there’s always something new happening among the stars - whether man made or natural.

  • The US has approved a plan by Elon Musk’s company SpaceX to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space. The plan, the first of its kind, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
  • The first images of an asteroid deliberately hit by a NASA spacecraft were revealed this week. Space vehicle Hera is now scouring the scene of the 2022 impact with Dimorphos, a test of the Earth’s defences against
  • NASA will also launch a new mission next year called Surveyor to further track potentially hazardous near Earth asteroids and comets.
  • Next summer four astronauts will fly into low Earth orbit to test docking equipment ahead of a proposed new moon landing in 2028.
  • 2027 will also see US company Vast plan to launch the first commercial space station.
